'''''Trypanosoma brucei''''' is a species of parasitic [[Kinetoplastida|kinetoplastid]] belonging to the genus ''[[Trypanosoma]]'' that is present in [[sub-Saharan Africa]]. Unlike other [[protozoan]] parasites that normally infect blood and tissue cells, it is exclusively extracellular and inhabits the [[blood plasma]] and body fluids.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Romero-Meza |first1=Gabriela |last2=Mugnier |first2=Monica R. |date=2020 |title=Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Trends in Parasitology |volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=571–572 |doi=10.1016/j.pt.2019.10.007 |pmc=7375462 |pmid=31757771}}</ref> It causes deadly vector-borne diseases: [[African trypanosomiasis]] or sleeping sickness in humans, and [[animal trypanosomiasis]] or ''nagana'' in cattle and horses.<ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Luzak V, López-Escobar L, Siegel TN, Figueiredo LM |date=October 2021 |title=Cell-to-Cell Heterogeneity in Trypanosomes |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |publisher=[[Annual Reviews (publisher)|Annual Reviews]] |volume=75 |issue=1 |pages=107–128 |doi=10.1146/annurev-micro-040821-012953 |pmid=34228491 |s2cid=235759288 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It is a [[species complex]] grouped into five subspecies: ''[[Trypanosoma brucei brucei|T. b. brucei]]'', ''[[Trypanosoma brucei equiperdum|T. b. equiperdum]]'', ''[[Trypanosoma brucei evansi|T. b. evansi]]'', ''[[Trypanosoma brucei gambiense|T. b. gambiense]]'' and ''[[Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense|T. b. rhodesiense]]''. The first is a parasite of non-human mammals and causes ''nagana'', while the latter two are zoonotic infecting both humans and animals and cause African trypanosomiasis.

''T. brucei'' is transmitted between mammal hosts by an [[insect]] [[Vector (epidemiology)|vector]] belonging to different species of [[tsetse fly]] (''Glossina''). Transmission occurs by biting during the insect's blood meal. The parasites undergo complex morphological changes as they move between insect and mammal over the course of [[#Life cycle|their life cycle]]. The mammalian bloodstream forms are notable for their cell surface proteins, [[variant surface glycoproteins]], which undergo remarkable [[antigenic variation]], enabling persistent evasion of host adaptive immunity leading to chronic infection. ''T. brucei'' is one of only a few pathogens known to cross the [[blood-brain barrier]].<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Masocha W, Kristensson K |year=2012 |title=Passage of parasites across the blood-brain barrier |journal=Virulence |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=202–212 |doi=10.4161/viru.19178 |pmc=3396699 |pmid=22460639}}</ref> There is an urgent need for the development of new drug therapies, as current treatments can have severe side effects and can prove fatal to the patient.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Legros D, Ollivier G, Gastellu-Etchegorry M, Paquet C, Burri C, Jannin J, Büscher P |date=July 2002 |title=Treatment of human African trypanosomiasis--present situation and needs for research and development |journal=The Lancet. Infectious Diseases |volume=2 |issue=7 |pages=437–440 |doi=10.1016/S1473-3099(02)00321-3 |pmid=12127356 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10144/18268}}</ref>

Whilst not historically regarded as ''T. brucei'' subspecies due to their different means of transmission, clinical presentation, and loss of [[kinetoplast]] DNA, genetic analyses reveal that ''T. b. equiperdum'' and ''T. b. evansi'' are evolved from parasites very similar to ''T. b. brucei'', and are thought to be members of the ''brucei'' [[clade]].<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Gibson W |date=July 2007 |title=Resolution of the species problem in African trypanosomes |journal=International Journal for Parasitology |volume=37 |issue=8–9 |pages=829–838 |doi=10.1016/j.ijpara.2007.03.002 |pmid=17451719}}</ref>

The parasite was discovered in 1894 by Sir [[David Bruce (microbiologist)|David Bruce]], after whom the scientific name was given in 1899.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Joubert JJ, Schutte CH, Irons DJ, Fripp PJ |year=1993 |title=Ubombo and the site of David Bruce's discovery of Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene |volume=87 |issue=4 |pages=494–495 |doi=10.1016/0035-9203(93)90056-v |pmid=8249096}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Cook GC |year=1994 |title=Sir David Bruce's elucidation of the aetiology of nagana--exactly one hundred years ago |journal=Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene |volume=88 |issue=3 |pages=257–258 |doi=10.1016/0035-9203(94)90068-x |pmid=7974656 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== History and discovery ==

=== Early records ===
Sleeping sickness in animals was described in ancient Egyptian writings. During the Middle Ages, Arabian traders noted the prevalence of sleeping sickness among Africans and their dogs.<ref name=":04">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Steverding D |date=February 2008 |title=The history of African trypanosomiasis |journal=Parasites & Vectors |volume=1 |issue=1 |page=3 |doi=10.1186/1756-3305-1-3 |pmc=2270819 |pmid=18275594 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It was a major infectious disease in southern and eastern Africa in the 19th century.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Berrang-Ford L, Odiit M, Maiso F, Waltner-Toews D, McDermott J |date=December 2006 |title=Sleeping sickness in Uganda: revisiting current and historical distributions |url=https://www.ajol.info/index.php/ahs/article/view/6958 |journal=African Health Sciences |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=223–231 |pmc=1832067 |pmid=17604511 |archive-date=30 September 2022 |access-date=30 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220930115822/https://www.ajol.info/index.php/ahs/article/view/6958 |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Zulu Kingdom]] (now part of South Africa) was severely struck by the disease, which became known to the British as ''[[nagana]]'',<ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" /> a [[Zulu language|Zulu]] word meaning "low or depressed in spirit". In other parts of Africa, Europeans called it the "fly disease".<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T8CWvVGwKhoC |title=Medical and Veterinary Entomology |vauthors=Mullen GR, Durden LA |date=2009 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-08-091969-0 |edition=2 |page=297 |language=en |archive-date=1 October 2024 |access-date=17 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241001183630/https://books.google.com/books?id=T8CWvVGwKhoC |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/b21364655/page/n13/mode/2up |title=Preliminary Report on the Tsetse Fly Disease or Nagana, in Zululand |vauthors=Bruce D |publisher=Bennett & Davis |year=1895 |location=Durban (South Africa) |page=1}}</ref>
[[File:An inhabitant of Buruma Island, Uganda, suffering from sleep Wellcome V0029100.jpg|thumb|A man having sleeping sickness at Buruma Island, Uganda.]]
John Aktins, an English naval surgeon, gave the first medical description of human sleeping sickness in 1734. He attributed deaths, which he called "sleepy distemper", in Guinea  to the infection.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Kennedy PG |date=February 2004 |title=Human African trypanosomiasis of the CNS: current issues and challenges |journal=The Journal of Clinical Investigation |volume=113 |issue=4 |pages=496–504 |doi=10.1172/JCI34802 |pmc=2214720 |pmid=14966556}}</ref> Another English physician, [[Thomas Masterman Winterbottom]], gave a clearer description of the symptoms from [[Sierra Leone]] in 1803.<ref name=":42">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Cox FE |date=June 2004 |title=History of sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis) |journal=Infectious Disease Clinics of North America |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=231–245 |doi=10.1016/j.idc.2004.01.004 |pmid=15145378}}</ref> Winterbottom described a key feature of the disease, swollen posterior cervical lymph nodes, and slaves who developed such swellings were ruled unfit for trade.<ref name=":3" /> The symptom is eponymously known as "[[Winterbottom's sign]]".<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Ormerod WE |date=October 1991 |title=Hypothesis: the significance of Winterbottom's sign |journal=The Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene |volume=94 |issue=5 |pages=338–340 |pmid=1942213}}</ref>

=== Discovery of the parasite ===
The [[Royal Army Medical Corps]] appointed [[David Bruce (microbiologist)|David Bruce]], who at the time was assistant professor of pathology at the [[Netley Hospital|Army Medical School in Netley]] with a rank of Captain in the army, in 1894 to investigate a disease known as ''nagana'' in South Africa. The disease caused severe problems among the local cattle and British Army horses.<ref name="Baker1995">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Baker JR |date=March 1995 |title=The subspecific taxonomy of Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Parasite |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=3–12 |doi=10.1051/parasite/1995021003 |pmid=9137639 |doi-access=free}} {{open access}}</ref> On 27 October 1894, Bruce and his microbiologist-wife Mary Elizabeth Bruce (''née'' Steele) moved to [[Lebombo Mountains|Ubombo Hill]], where the disease was most prevalent.<ref name="cook">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iB_ibIXxhOMC&q=tropical+medicine+illustrated |title=Tropical Medicine: An Illustrated History of The Pioneers |vauthors=Cook GC |date=2007 |publisher=Elsevier Ltd. |isbn=978-0-08-055939-1 |location=Burlington (US) |pages=145–156 |archive-date=1 October 2024 |access-date=26 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241001183634/https://books.google.com/books?id=iB_ibIXxhOMC&q=tropical+medicine+illustrated#v=snippet&q=tropical%20medicine%20illustrated&f=false |url-status=live }}</ref>

On the sixth day of investigation, Bruce identified parasites from the blood of diseased cows. He initially noted them as a kind of filaria (tiny roundworms), but by the end of the year established that the parasites were "haematozoa" (protozoan) and were the cause of ''nagana''.<ref name="Baker1995" /> It was the discovery of ''Trypanosoma brucei.''<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Ellis H |date=March 2006 |title=Sir David Bruce, a pioneer of tropical medicine |journal=British Journal of Hospital Medicine |volume=67 |issue=3 |page=158 |doi=10.12968/hmed.2006.67.3.20624 |pmid=16562450}}</ref> The scientific name was created by British zoologists [[Henry George Plimmer]] and [[John Rose Bradford]] in 1899 as ''Trypanosoma brucii'' due to printer's error.<ref name="Baker1995" /><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Martini E |date=1903 |title=Ueber die Entwickelung der Tsetseparasiten in Säugethieren |trans-title=Preliminary note on the morphology and distribution of the parasite found in tsetse disease |journal=Zeitschrift für Hygiene und Infektionskrankheiten |language=de |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=341–351 |doi=10.1007/BF02217469 |s2cid=12816407}}</ref> The genus ''Trypanosoma'' was already introduced by Hungarian physician David Gruby in his description of ''T. sanguinis,'' a species he discovered in frogs in 1843.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Novy FG |date=1907 |title=Trypanosomes |journal=Journal of the American Medical Association |language=en |volume=XLVIII |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1001/jama.1907.25220270001001}}</ref>

=== Sleeping Sickness Commission ===
{{Main|Sleeping Sickness Commission}}
The [[Royal Society]] constituted a three-member Sleeping Sickness Commission on 10 May 1902 to investigate the epidemic in Uganda.<ref name=":52">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Boyd J |date=June 1973 |title=Sleeping sickness. The Castellani-Bruce controversy |journal=Notes and Records of the Royal Society of London |volume=28 |pages=93–110 |doi=10.1098/rsnr.1973.0008 |pmid=11615538 |s2cid=37631020}}</ref> The Commission comprised [[George Carmichael Low]] from the London [[London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine|School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine]] as the leader, his colleague [[Aldo Castellani]] and [[Cuthbert Christy]], a medical officer on duty in Bombay, India.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Cook GC |date=January 1993 |title=George Carmichael Low FRCP: an underrated figure in British tropical medicine |journal=Journal of the Royal College of Physicians of London |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=81–82 |pmc=5396591 |pmid=8426352 |doi=10.1016/S0035-8819(25)01075-X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Cook GC |date=1993 |title=Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene meeting at Manson House, London, 10 December 1992. George Carmichael Low FRCP: twelfth president of the Society and underrated pioneer of tropical medicine |journal=Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene |volume=87 |issue=4 |pages=355–360 |doi=10.1016/0035-9203(93)90002-8 |pmid=8249057}}</ref> At the time, a debate remained on the etiology, some favoured bacterial infection while some believed as [[helminth infection]].<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Amaral I |date=December 2012 |title=Bacteria or parasite? the controversy over the etiology of sleeping sickness and the Portuguese participation, 1898-1904 |journal=Historia, Ciencias, Saude--Manguinhos |volume=19 |issue=4 |pages=1275–1300 |doi=10.1590/s0104-59702012005000004 |pmid=23184240 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The first investigation focussed on ''Filaria perstans'' (later renamed ''[[Mansonella perstans]]''), a small roundworm transmitted by flies, and bacteria as possible causes, only to discover that the epidemic was not related to these pathogens.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Cook GC |date=May 2012 |title=Patrick Manson (1844-1922) FRS: Filaria (Mansonella) perstans and sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis) |journal=Journal of Medical Biography |volume=20 |issue=2 |page=69 |doi=10.1258/jmb.2010.010051 |pmid=22791871 |s2cid=33661530}}</ref><ref name=":72">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Lumsden WH |date=August 1974 |title=Some episodes in the history of African trypanosomiasis |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine |volume=67 |issue=8 |pages=789–796 |doi=10.1177/003591577406700846 |pmc=1645813 |pmid=4607392}}</ref> The team was described as an "ill-assorted group"<ref name=":72" /> and a "queer lot",<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Wiggins CA |date=November 1960 |title=Early days in East Africa and Uganda |journal=East African Medical Journal |volume=37 |pages=699–708 contd |pmid=13785176}}</ref> and the expedition "a failure".<ref name=":63" /> Low, whose conduct was described as "truculent and prone to take offence", left the Commission and Africa after three months.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Davies JN |date=March 1962 |title=The cause of sleeping-sickness? Entebbe 1902-03. I |journal=East African Medical Journal |volume=39 |pages=81–99 |pmid=13883839}}</ref>

In February 1902, the [[British War Office]], following a request from the Royal Society, appointed David Bruce to lead the second Sleeping Sickness Commission.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last=J.R. B. |date=1932 |title=Sir David Bruce. 1855-1931 |journal=Obituary Notices of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=79–85 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.1932.0017  |doi-access=free|issn=1479-571X |jstor=768965}}</ref> With [[David Nunes Nabarro]] (from the [[University College Hospital]]), Bruce and his wife joined Castellani and Christy on 16 March.<ref name=":72" /> In November 1902, Castellani had found the trypanosomes in the [[cerebrospinal fluid]] of an infected person. He was convinced that the trypanosome was the causative parasite of sleeping sickness. Like Low, his conduct has been criticised and the Royal Society refused to publish his report. He was further infuriated when Bruce advised him not to make rash conclusion without further evidences, as there were many other parasites to consider.<ref name=":52" /> Castellani left Africa in April and published his report as "On the discovery of a species of ''Trypanosoma'' in the cerebrospinal fluid of cases of sleeping sickness" in ''[[The Lancet]].''<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Castellani A |date=1903 |title=On the discovery of a species of trypanosoma in the cerebrospinal fluid of cases of sleeping sickness |journal=The Lancet |language=en |volume=161 |issue=4164 |pages=1735–1736 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(01)70338-8}}</ref> By then the Royal Society had already published the report.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Castellani A |date=1903 |title=On the discovery of a species of ''trypanosoma'' in the cerebrospinal fluid of cases of sleeping sickness |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London |language=en |volume=71 |issue=467–476 |pages=501–508 |doi=10.1098/rspl.1902.0134 |s2cid=59110369}}</ref> By August 1903, Bruce and his team established that the disease was transmitted by the [[tsetse fly]], ''Glossina palpalis.''<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Welburn SC, Maudlin I, Simarro PP |date=December 2009 |title=Controlling sleeping sickness - a review |url=http://doc.rero.ch/record/298806/files/S0031182009006416.pdf |journal=Parasitology |volume=136 |issue=14 |pages=1943–1949 |doi=10.1017/S0031182009006416 |pmid=19691861 |s2cid=41052902 |archive-date=10 February 2023 |access-date=30 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210110307/https://doc.rero.ch/record/298806/files/S0031182009006416.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> However, Bruce did not understand the trypanosoma life cycle and believed that the parasites were simply transmitted from one person to another.<ref name=":04" />

=== Discovery of human trypanosomes ===
British Colonial Surgeon Robert Michael Forde was the first to find the parasite in human. He found it from an English steamboat captain who was admitted to a hospital at Bathurst, Gambia, in 1901.<ref name=":04" /> His report in 1902 indicates that he believed it to be a kind of filarial worm.<ref name=":42" /> From the same person, Forde's colleague Joseph Everett Dutton identified it as a protozoan belonging to the genus ''Trypanosoma.<ref name="Baker1995" />'' Knowing the distinct features, Dutton proposed a new species name in 1902:
{{Blockquote|At present then it is impossible to decide definitely as to the species, but if on further study it should be found to differ from other disease-producing trypanosomes I would suggest that it be called ''Trypanosoma gambiense.''<ref>{{Cite web |date=1902 |title=Preliminary note upon a trypanosome occurring in the blood of man |url=https://wellcomecollection.org/works/w3s9ydrt |access-date=2021-03-21 |website=Wellcome Collection |language=en |vauthors=Dutton JE |archive-date=31 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221031172753/https://wellcomecollection.org/works/w3s9ydrt |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

Another human trypanosome (now called ''T. brucei rhodesiense'') was discovered by British parasitologists John William Watson Stephens and Harold Benjamin Fantham.<ref name=":04" /> In 1910, Stephens noted in his experimental infection in rats that the trypanosome, obtained from an individual from [[Northern Rhodesia]] (later Zambia), was not the same as ''T. gambiense''. The source of the parasite, an Englishman travelling in Rhodesia was found with the blood parasites in 1909, and was transported to and admitted at the [[Royal Southern Hospital]] in Liverpool under the care of [[Ronald Ross]].<ref name="Baker1995" />  Fantham described the parasite's morphology and found that it was a different trypanosome.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Stephens JW, Fantham HB, Ross R |date=1910 |title=On the peculiar morphology of a trypanosome from a case of sleeping sickness and the possibility of its being a new species (''T. rhodesiense'') |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series B |volume=83 |issue=561 |pages=28–33 |doi=10.1098/rspb.1910.0064 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Stephens JW, Fantham HB |date=1910 |title=On the Peculiar Morphology of a Trypanosome From a Case of Sleeping Sickness and the Possibility of Its Being a New Species (''T. Rhodesiense'') |url=https://zenodo.org/record/1429906 |journal=Annals of Tropical Medicine & Parasitology |language=en |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=343–350 |doi=10.1080/00034983.1910.11685723 |archive-date=3 October 2022 |access-date=30 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221003083958/https://zenodo.org/record/1429906 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Subspecies==
''T. brucei'' is a species complex that includes:<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kostygov |first1=Alexei Y. |last2=Karnkowska |first2=Anna |last3=Votýpka |first3=Jan |last4=Tashyreva |first4=Daria |last5=Maciszewski |first5=Kacper |last6=Yurchenko |first6=Vyacheslav |last7=Lukeš |first7=Julius |date=2021-03-10 |title=Euglenozoa: taxonomy, diversity and ecology, symbioses and viruses |journal=Open Biology |volume=11 |issue=3 |article-number=200407 |doi=10.1098/rsob.200407 |pmc=8061765 |doi-access=free |pmid=33715388 }}</ref>

=== Etymology ===
The genus name is derived from two Greek words:  τρυπανον (''trypanon'' or ''trupanon''), which means "borer" or "auger", referring to the corkscrew-like movement;<ref name=":0" /> and σῶμα (''sôma''), meaning "body".<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2006 |title=Etymologia: Trypanosoma |journal=Emerging Infectious Diseases |volume=12 |issue=9 |page=1473 |doi=10.3201/eid1209.ET1209 |issn=1080-6040 |pmc=3293449}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Morriswood |first=Brooke |date=2015 |title=Form, Fabric, and Function of a Flagellum-Associated Cytoskeletal Structure |journal=Cells |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=726–747 |doi=10.3390/cells4040726 |issn=2073-4409 |pmc=4695855 |pmid=26540076 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The specific name is after David Bruce, who discovered the parasites in 1894.<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" /> The subspecies, the human strains, are named after the regions in Africa where they were first identified: ''T. brucei gambiense'' was described from an Englishman in Gambia in 1901; ''T. brucei rhodesiense'' was found from another Englishman in Northern Rhodesia in 1909.<ref name="Baker1995" />

==Structure==
[[Image:TrypanosomaBrucei ProcyclicTrypomastigote SEM.jpg|thumb|right|250px| [[Scanning electron microscope|SEM]] false colour [[micrograph]] of the [[Procyclic life stage|procyclic form]] as found in the tsetse fly midgut. The cell body is shown in orange and the flagellum is in red. 84 pixels/μm.]]''T. brucei'' is a typical unicellular [[eukaryotic cell]], and measures 8 to 50 μm in length. It has an elongated body having a streamlined and tapered shape. Its [[cell membrane]] (called pellicle) encloses the cell organelles, including the [[cell nucleus|nucleus]], [[mitochondria]], [[endoplasmic reticulum]], [[Golgi apparatus]], and [[ribosomes]]. In addition, there is an unusual organelle called the [[kinetoplast]], which is a complex of thousands of interlinked circles of mitochondrial DNA known as mini- and maxicircles.<ref name="Amodeo-et-al-2018">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Amodeo S, Jakob M, Ochsenreiter T |date=April 2018 |title=Characterization of the novel mitochondrial genome replication factor MiRF172 in ''Trypanosoma brucei'' |journal=Journal of Cell Science |publisher=[[The Company of Biologists]] |volume=131 |issue=8 |article-number=jcs211730 |doi=10.1242/jcs.211730 |pmc=5963845 |pmid=29626111 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The kinetoplast lies near the [[basal body]] with which it is indistinguishable under microscope. From the basal body arises a single [[flagellum]] that run towards the anterior end. Along the body surface, the flagellum is attached to the cell membrane forming an undulating membrane. Only the tip of the flagellum is free at the anterior end.<ref name="fao">{{Cite web |title=African animal trypanosomes |url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/006/x0413e/x0413e02.htm#ref1.2.1.1 |access-date=28 January 2016 |publisher=Food and Agricultural Organization |archive-date=3 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160203150518/http://www.fao.org/docrep/006/x0413e/x0413e02.htm#ref1.2.1.1 |url-status=live }}</ref> The cell surface of the bloodstream form features a dense coat of variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) which is replaced by an equally dense coat of [[procyclin]]s when the parasite differentiates into the [[procyclic life stage|procyclic phase]] in the tsetse fly midgut.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Romero-Meza G, Mugnier MR |date=June 2020 |title=''Trypanosoma brucei'' |journal=Trends in Parasitology |volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=571–572 |doi=10.1016/j.pt.2019.10.007 |pmc=7375462 |pmid=31757771}}</ref>

[[File:TrypanosomatidMorphologies PlainSVG.svg|thumb|right|The six main morphologies of trypanosomatids. The different life cycle stages of ''T brucei'' fall into the trypomastigote and epimastigote morphological categories.]]
[[Trypanosomatida|Trypanosomatids]] show several different classes of cellular organisation of which two are adopted by ''T. brucei'' at different stages of the life cycle:<ref name=fao/>
* [[Trypanosomatida#Morphologies|Epimastigote]], which is found in tsetse fly. Its kinetoplast and basal body lie anterior to the nucleus, with a long flagellum attached along the cell body. The flagellum starts from the centre of the body.
* [[Trypanosomatida#Morphologies|Trypomastigote]], which is found in mammalian hosts. The kinetoplast and basal body are posterior of nucleus. The flagellum arises from the posterior end of the body.
[[Image:Trypanosome Flagellum Structure.png|thumbnail|Flagellar structure]]
These names are derived from the [[Ancient Greek|Greek]] ''mastig-'' meaning [[whip]], referring to the trypanosome's whip-like flagellum. The trypanosome flagellum has two main structures. It is made up of a typical flagellar axoneme, which lies parallel to the [[paraflagellar rod]],<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Koyfman AY, Schmid MF, Gheiratmand L, Fu CJ, Khant HA, Huang D, He CY, Chiu W |date=July 2011 |title=Structure of Trypanosoma brucei flagellum accounts for its bihelical motion |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=108 |issue=27 |pages=11105–11108 |bibcode=2011PNAS..10811105K |doi=10.1073/pnas.1103634108 |pmc=3131312 |pmid=21690369 |doi-access=free}}</ref> a lattice structure of proteins unique to the [[kinetoplastida|kinetoplastids]], [[euglenoid]]s and [[dinoflagellate]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=v |date=1988 |title=The paraflagellar rod: a structure in search of a function |journal=Biology of the Cell |language=en |volume=63 |issue=2 |pages=169–181 |doi=10.1016/0248-4900(88)90056-1 |issn=0248-4900 |s2cid=86009836}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Bastin P, Matthews KR, Gull K |date=August 1996 |title=The paraflagellar rod of kinetoplastida: solved and unsolved questions |journal=Parasitology Today |volume=12 |issue=8 |pages=302–307 |doi=10.1016/0169-4758(96)10031-4 |pmid=15275181}}</ref>

The [[microtubule]]s of the flagellar [[axoneme]] lie in the normal 9+2 arrangement, orientated with the + at the anterior end and the − in the basal body. The cytoskeletal structure extends from the basal body to the kinetoplast. The flagellum is bound to the cytoskeleton of the main cell body by four specialised microtubules, which run parallel and in the same direction to the flagellar tubulin.<ref name="Sunter-Gull-2016">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Sunter JD, Gull K |date=April 2016 |title=The Flagellum Attachment Zone: 'The Cellular Ruler' of Trypanosome Morphology |journal=Trends in Parasitology |publisher=[[Cell Press]] |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=309–324 |doi=10.1016/j.pt.2015.12.010 |pmc=4827413 |pmid=26776656 |s2cid=1080165}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Woods A, Sherwin T, Sasse R, MacRae TH, Baines AJ, Gull K |date=July 1989 |title=Definition of individual components within the cytoskeleton of Trypanosoma brucei by a library of monoclonal antibodies |journal=Journal of Cell Science |volume=93 |issue=3 |pages=491–500 |doi=10.1242/jcs.93.3.491 |pmid=2606940}}</ref>

The flagellar function is twofold — locomotion via oscillations along the attached flagellum and cell body in human blood stream and tsetse fly gut,<ref name="lang">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Langousis G, Hill KL |date=July 2014 |title=Motility and more: the flagellum of Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Nature Reviews. Microbiology |volume=12 |issue=7 |pages=505–518 |doi=10.1038/nrmicro3274 |pmc=4278896 |pmid=24931043}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Halliday C, de Castro-Neto A, Alcantara CL, Cunha-E-Silva NL, Vaughan S, Sunter JD |date=April 2021 |title=Trypanosomatid Flagellar Pocket from Structure to Function |journal=Trends in Parasitology |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=317–329 |doi=10.1016/j.pt.2020.11.005 |pmid=33308952 |s2cid=229179306}}</ref> and attachment to the salivary gland epithelium of the fly during the epimastigote stage.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Krüger T, Schuster S, Engstler M |date=December 2018 |title=Beyond Blood: African Trypanosomes on the Move |journal=Trends in Parasitology |volume=34 |issue=12 |pages=1056–1067 |doi=10.1016/j.pt.2018.08.002 |pmid=30181072 |s2cid=52154369}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Ralston KS, Kabututu ZP, Melehani JH, Oberholzer M, Hill KL |date=2009 |title=The Trypanosoma brucei flagellum: moving parasites in new directions |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |volume=63 |pages=335–362 |doi=10.1146/annurev.micro.091208.073353 |pmc=3821760 |pmid=19575562}}</ref> The flagellum propels the body in such a way that the axoneme generates the oscillation and a flagellar wave is created along the undulating membrane. As a result, the body moves in a corkscrew pattern.<ref name=":0" /> In flagella of other organisms, the movement starts from the base towards the tip, while in ''T. brucei'' and other trypanosomatids, the beat originates from the tip and progresses towards the base, forcing the body to move towards the direction of the tip of the flagellum.<ref name=":4" />

==Life cycle==
[[File:Trypanosoma brucei Life Cycle.svg|thumb|right|Life cycle]]
''T. brucei'' completes its life cycle between tsetse fly (of the genus ''Glossina'') and mammalian hosts, including humans, cattle, horses, and wild animals. In stressful environments, ''T. brucei'' produces [[exosome (vesicle)|exosome]]s containing the [[spliced leader RNA]] and uses the [[endosomal sorting complexes required for transport]] (ESCRT) system to [[secretion|secrete]] them as [[extracellular vesicle]]s.<ref name="Juan-Furthauer-2018">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Juan T, Fürthauer M |date=February 2018 |title=Biogenesis and function of ESCRT-dependent extracellular vesicles |journal=Seminars in Cell & Developmental Biology |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |volume=74 |pages=66–77 |doi=10.1016/j.semcdb.2017.08.022 |pmid=28807885}}</ref> When absorbed by other trypanosomes these EVs cause repulsive movement away from the area and so away from bad environments.<ref name="Juan-Furthauer-2018" />

===In mammalian host===
Infection occurs when a vector tsetse fly bites a mammalian host. The fly injects the metacyclic trypomastigotes into the skin tissue. The trypomastigotes enter the [[lymphatic system]] and into the bloodstream. The initial trypomastigotes are short and stumpy (SS).<ref name="kdc">{{Cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UknhQgAACAAJ |title=Parasitology (Protozoology and Helminthology) in relation to clinical medicine |vauthors=Chatterjee KD |date=2009 |publisher=CBC Publishers |isbn=978-8-12-39-1810-5 |edition=13 |location=New Delhi |pages=56–57 |archive-date=1 October 2024 |access-date=22 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241001183629/https://books.google.com/books?id=UknhQgAACAAJ |url-status=live }}</ref> They are protected from the host's immune system by producing antigentic variation called [[variant surface glycoproteins]] on their body surface.<ref name=":9" /> Once inside the bloodstream, they grow into long and slender forms (LS). Then, they multiply by [[Fission (biology)|binary fission]]. Some of the daughter cells then become short and stumpy again.<ref name="cdc">{{Cite web |title=Parasites - African Trypanosomiasis (also known as Sleeping Sickness) |url=https://www.cdc.gov/parasites/sleepingsickness/biology.html |access-date=29 January 2016 |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention |archive-date=1 February 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160201213414/http://www.cdc.gov/parasites/sleepingsickness/biology.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Seed-Wenck-2003">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Seed JR, Wenck MA |date=June 2003 |title=Role of the long slender to short stumpy transition in the life cycle of the african trypanosomes |journal=Kinetoplastid Biology and Disease |publisher=[[BioMed Central]] |volume=2 |issue=1 |article-number=3 |doi=10.1186/1475-9292-2-3 |pmc=165594 |pmid=12844365 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" /> Some of them remains as intermediate forms, representing a transitional stage between the long and short forms.<ref name=":10" /> The long slender forms are able to penetrate the blood vessel endothelium and invade extravascular tissues, including the [[central nervous system]] (CNS)<ref name=lang/> and placenta in pregnant women.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McClure |first1=Elizabeth M. |last2=Goldenberg |first2=Robert L. |date=2009 |title=Infection and stillbirth |journal=Seminars in Fetal & Neonatal Medicine |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=182–189 |doi=10.1016/j.siny.2009.02.003 |issn=1878-0946 |pmc=3962114 |pmid=19285457}}</ref>

Sometimes, wild animals can be infected by the tsetse fly and they act as reservoirs. In these animals, they do not produce the disease, but the live parasite can be transmitted back to the normal hosts.<ref name="kdc" /> Besides preparation to be taken up and vectored to another host by a tsetse fly, transition from LS to SS in the mammal serves to prolong the host's lifespan {{endash}} controlling [[parasitemia]] aids in increasing the total transmitting duration of any particular infested host.<ref name="Seed-Wenck-2003" /><ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" />

===In tsetse fly===
Unlike [[Anopheles|anopheline mosquitos]] and [[sandflies]] that transmit other protozoan infections in which only females are involved, both sexes of tsetse flies are blood feeders and equally transmit trypanosomes.<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last1=Rotureau |first1=Brice |last2=Van Den Abbeele |first2=Jan |date=2013 |title=Through the dark continent: African trypanosome development in the tsetse fly |journal=Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology |volume=3 |page=53 |doi=10.3389/fcimb.2013.00053 |issn=2235-2988 |pmc=3776139 |pmid=24066283 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The short and stumpy trypomastigotes (SS) are taken up by tsetse flies during a blood meal.<ref name="Seed-Wenck-2003" /><ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" /> Survival in the tsetse midgut is one reason for the particular adaptations of the SS stage.<ref name="Seed-Wenck-2003" /><ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" /> The trypomastigotes enter the midgut of the fly where they become procyclic trypomastigotes as they replace their VSG with other protein coats called [[procyclins]].<ref name=":9" /> Because the fly faces digestive damage from [[immune factor]]s in the [[hematophagy|bloodmeal]], it produces [[serpin]]s to suppress the infection. The serpins including ''[[GmmSRPN3]]'', ''[[GmmSRPN5]]'', ''[[GmmSRPN9]]'', and especially ''[[GmmSRPN10]]'' are then hijacked by the parasite to aid its own midgut infection, using them to inactivate bloodmeal [[trypanolytic]] factors which would otherwise make the fly host inhospitable.<ref name="Mideo-et-al-2013">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Mideo N, Acosta-Serrano A, Aebischer T, Brown MJ, Fenton A, Friman VP, Restif O, Reece SE, Webster JP, Brown SP |date=January 2013 |title=Life in cells, hosts, and vectors: parasite evolution across scales |url=https://researchonline.rvc.ac.uk/id/eprint/8749/1/8749.pdf |journal=Infection, Genetics and Evolution |volume=13 |pages=344–347 |doi=10.1016/j.meegid.2012.03.016 |pmid=22465537 |bibcode=2013InfGE..13..344M |archive-date=2 July 2023 |access-date=23 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702061440/https://rvc-repository.worktribe.com/ |url-status=live }} {{small|1=(VPF [[ORCID]] [http://orcid.org/0000-0002-1592-157X 0000-0002-1592-157X])}}.</ref>{{rp|346}}

The procyclic trypomastigotes cross the peritrophic matrix, undergo slight elongation and migrate to the anterior part of the midgut as non-proliferative long mesocyclic trypomastigotes. As they reach the proventriculus, they became thinner and undergo cytoplasmic rearrangement to give rise to proliferative epimastigotes.<ref name=":11" /> The epimastigotes divide asymmetrically to produce long and short epimastigotes. The long epimastigote cannot move to other places and simply die off by [[apoptosis]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Proto |first1=William R. |last2=Coombs |first2=Graham H. |last3=Mottram |first3=Jeremy C. |date=2013 |title=Cell death in parasitic protozoa: regulated or incidental? |journal=Nature Reviews. Microbiology |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=58–66 |doi=10.1038/nrmicro2929 |issn=1740-1534 |pmid=23202528 |s2cid=1633550}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Van Den Abbeele |first1=J. |last2=Claes |first2=Y. |last3=van Bockstaele |first3=D. |last4=Le Ray |first4=D. |last5=Coosemans |first5=M. |date=1999 |title=Trypanosoma brucei spp. development in the tsetse fly: characterization of the post-mesocyclic stages in the foregut and proboscis |journal=Parasitology |volume=118 |issue=5 |pages=469–478 |doi=10.1017/s0031182099004217 |issn=0031-1820 |pmid=10363280 |s2cid=32217938}}</ref> The short epimastigote migrate from the proventriculus via the foregut and proboscis to the [[salivary gland]]s where they get attached to the salivary gland epithelium.<ref name=":0" /> Even all the short forms do not succeed in the complete migration to the salivary glands as most of them perish on the way–only up to five may survive.<ref name=":11" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Oberle |first1=Michael |last2=Balmer |first2=Oliver |last3=Brun |first3=Reto |last4=Roditi |first4=Isabel |date=2010 |title=Bottlenecks and the maintenance of minor genotypes during the life cycle of Trypanosoma brucei |journal=PLOS Pathogens |volume=6 |issue=7 |article-number=e1001023 |doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.1001023 |issn=1553-7374 |pmc=2912391 |pmid=20686656 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In the salivary glands, the survivors undergo phases of reproduction. The first cycle in an equal mitosis by which a mother cell produces two similar daughter epimastigotes. They remain attach to the epithelium. This phase is the main reproduction in first-stage infection to ensure sufficient number of parasites in the salivary gland.<ref name=":11" /> The second cycle, which usually occurs in late-stage infection, involves unequal mitosis that produces two different daughter cells from the mother epimastigote. One daughter is an epimastigote that remains non-infective and the other is a trypomastigote.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rotureau |first1=Brice |last2=Subota |first2=Ines |last3=Buisson |first3=Johanna |last4=Bastin |first4=Philippe |date=2012 |title=A new asymmetric division contributes to the continuous production of infective trypanosomes in the tsetse fly |journal=Development |volume=139 |issue=10 |pages=1842–1850 |doi=10.1242/dev.072611 |issn=1477-9129 |pmid=22491946 |s2cid=7068417 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The trypomastigote detach from the epithelium and undergo transformation into short and stumpy trypomastigotes. The surface procyclins are replaced with VSGs and become the infective metacyclic trypomastigotes.<ref name=":10" /> Complete development in the fly takes about 20 days.<ref name="kdc" /><ref name="cdc" /> They are injected into the mammalian host along with the saliva on biting, and are known as salivarian.<ref name=":11" />

In the case of ''T. b. brucei'' infecting ''Glossina palpalis gambiensis'', the parasite changes the [[proteome]] contents of the fly's head and causes behavioral changes such as unnecessarily increased feeding frequency, which increases transmission opportunities. This is related to altered [[glucose]] metabolism that causes a perceived need for more calories. (The metabolic change, in turn, being due to complete absence of [[Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase|glucose-6-phosphate 1-dehydrogenase]] in infected flies.) [[Monoamine neurotransmitter]] synthesis is also altered: production of [[aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase]] involved in [[dopamine]] and [[serotonin]] synthesis, and [[α-methyldopa hypersensitive protein]] was induced. This is similar to the alterations in other [[fly|dipteran]] vectors' head proteomes under infection by other eukaryotic parasites of mammals.<ref name="Lefevre-et-al-2007">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Lefèvre T, Thomas F, Ravel S, Patrel D, Renault L, Le Bourligu L, Cuny G, Biron DG |date=December 2007 |title=Trypanosoma brucei brucei induces alteration in the head proteome of the tsetse fly vector Glossina palpalis gambiensis |journal=Insect Molecular Biology |publisher=[[Royal Entomological Society]] ([[Wiley Publishing|Wiley]]) |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=651–660 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2583.2007.00761.x |pmid=18092995 |s2cid=3134104}}</ref>

==Reproduction==
===Binary fission===
[[Image:Trypanosome Cell Cycle.png|thumbnail|Trypanosome cell cycle (procyclic form)]]
The reproduction of ''T. brucei'' is unusual compared to most eukaryotes. The nuclear membrane remains intact and the chromosomes do not condense during mitosis. The basal body, unlike the [[centrosome]] of most eukaryotic cells, does not play a role in the organisation of the spindle and instead is involved in division of the kinetoplast. The events of reproduction are:<ref name=fao/>
# The basal body duplicates and both remain associated with the kinetoplast. Each basal body forms a separate flagellum.
# Kinetoplast DNA undergoes synthesis then the kinetoplast divides coupled with separation of the two basal bodies.
# [[Nuclear DNA]] undergoes synthesis while a new flagellum extends from the younger, more posterior, basal body.
# The nucleus undergoes mitosis.
# [[Cytokinesis]] progresses from the anterior to posterior.
# Division completes with [[abscission]].

===Meiosis===
In the 1980s, DNA analyses of the developmental stages of ''T. brucei'' started to indicate that the trypomastigote in the tsetse fly undergoes [[meiosis]], i.e., a sexual reproduction stage.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Zampetti-Bosseler F, Schweizer J, Pays E, Jenni L, Steinert M |date=August 1986 |title=Evidence for haploidy in metacyclic forms of Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=83 |issue=16 |pages=6063–6064 |bibcode=1986PNAS...83.6063Z |doi=10.1073/pnas.83.16.6063 |pmc=386438 |pmid=3461475 |doi-access=free}}</ref> But it is not always necessary for a complete life cycle.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Jenni L |date=1990 |title=Sexual stages in trypanosomes and implications |journal=Annales de Parasitologie Humaine et Comparée |volume=65 |issue=Suppl 1 |pages=19–21 |doi=10.1051/parasite/1990651019 |pmid=2264676 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The existence of meiosis-specific proteins was reported in 2011.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Peacock L, Ferris V, Sharma R, Sunter J, Bailey M, Carrington M, Gibson W |date=March 2011 |title=Identification of the meiotic life cycle stage of Trypanosoma brucei in the tsetse fly |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=108 |issue=9 |pages=3671–3676 |bibcode=2011PNAS..108.3671P |doi=10.1073/pnas.1019423108 |pmc=3048101 |pmid=21321215 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The haploid gametes (daughter cells produced after meiosis) were discovered in 2014. The haploid trypomastigote-like gametes can interact with each other via their flagella and undergo cell fusion (the process is called syngamy).<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Peacock L, Bailey M, Carrington M, Gibson W |date=January 2014 |title=Meiosis and haploid gametes in the pathogen Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Current Biology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=181–186 |bibcode=2014CBio...24..181P |doi=10.1016/j.cub.2013.11.044 |pmc=3928991 |pmid=24388851}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Peacock L, Ferris V, Bailey M, Gibson W |date=February 2014 |title=Mating compatibility in the parasitic protist Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Parasites & Vectors |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=78 |doi=10.1186/1756-3305-7-78 |pmc=3936861 |pmid=24559099 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Thus, in addition to binary fission, ''T. brucei'' can multiply by sexual reproduction. Trypanosomes belong to the supergroup [[Excavata]] and are one of the earliest diverging lineages among eukaryotes.<ref name="pmid19237557">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Hampl V, Hug L, Leigh JW, Dacks JB, Lang BF, Simpson AG, Roger AJ |date=March 2009 |title=Phylogenomic analyses support the monophyly of Excavata and resolve relationships among eukaryotic "supergroups" |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=106 |issue=10 |pages=3859–3864 |bibcode=2009PNAS..106.3859H |doi=10.1073/pnas.0807880106 |pmc=2656170 |pmid=19237557 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The discovery of sexual reproduction in ''T. brucei'' supports the hypothesis that meiosis and sexual reproduction are ancestral and ubiquitous features of eukaryotes.<ref name="pmid18663385">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Malik SB, Pightling AW, Stefaniak LM, Schurko AM, Logsdon JM |date=August 2007 |title=An expanded inventory of conserved meiotic genes provides evidence for sex in Trichomonas vaginalis |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=3 |issue=8 |article-number=e2879 |bibcode=2008PLoSO...3.2879M |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0002879 |pmc=2488364 |pmid=18663385 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Infection and pathogenicity==
{{Main|African trypanosomiasis}}

The insect vectors for ''T. brucei'' are different species of [[tsetse fly]] (genus ''Glossina''). The major vectors of ''T. b. gambiense'', causing West African sleeping sickness, are [[Glossina palpalis|''G. palpalis'']], [[Glossina tachinoides|''G. tachinoides'']], and [[Glossina fuscipes|''G. fuscipes'']]. While the principal vectors of ''T. b. rhodesiense'', causing East African sleeping sickness, are [[Glossina morsitans|''G. morsitans'']], [[Glossina pallidipes|''G. pallidipes'']], and [[Glossina swynnertoni|''G. swynnertoni'']]. Animal trypanosomiasis is transmitted by a dozen species of ''Glossina''.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Medical and Veterinary Entomology |vauthors=Krisnky WL |date=2009 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-0-80-91969-0 |veditors=Mullen GR, Durden L |edition=2 |location=Amsterdam |page=296 |chapter=Tsetse fly (Glossinidae) |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=T8CWvVGwKhoC |archive-date=1 October 2024 |access-date=17 September 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241001183630/https://books.google.com/books?id=T8CWvVGwKhoC |url-status=live }}</ref>

In later stages of a ''T. brucei'' infection of a mammalian host the parasite may migrate from the bloodstream to also infect the lymph and cerebrospinal fluids. It is under this tissue invasion that the parasites produce the sleeping sickness.<ref name=kdc/>

In addition to the major form of transmission via the tsetse fly, ''T. brucei'' may be transferred between mammals via bodily fluid exchange, such as by blood transfusion or sexual contact, although this is thought to be rare.<ref name="CDC_epi">{{Cite web |date=2017-05-02 |title=African Trypanosomes: epidemiology and risk factors |url=https://www.cdc.gov/parasites/sleepingsickness/epi.html |publisher=Centers for Disease Control |access-date=17 September 2017 |archive-date=2 July 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230702061441/https://www.cdc.gov/parasites/sleepingsickness/epi.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Rocha">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Rocha G, Martins A, Gama G, Brandão F, Atouguia J |date=January 2004 |title=Possible cases of sexual and congenital transmission of sleeping sickness |journal=Lancet |volume=363 |issue=9404 |page=247 |doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(03)15345-7 |pmid=14738812 |s2cid=5311361}}</ref> Newborn babies can be infected (vertical or congenital transmission) from infected mothers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lindner |first1=Andreas K. |last2=Priotto |first2=Gerardo |date=2010 |title=The unknown risk of vertical transmission in sleeping sickness--a literature review |journal=PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases |volume=4 |issue=12 |article-number=e783 |doi=10.1371/journal.pntd.0000783 |issn=1935-2735 |pmc=3006128 |pmid=21200416 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Chemotherapy==
There are four drugs generally recommended for the first-line treatment of African trypanosomiasis: [[suramin]] developed in 1921, [[pentamidine]] developed in 1941, [[melarsoprol]] developed in 1949 and [[eflornithine]] developed in 1990.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Nok AJ |date=May 2003 |title=Arsenicals (melarsoprol), pentamidine and suramin in the treatment of human African trypanosomiasis |journal=Parasitology Research |volume=90 |issue=1 |pages=71–79 |doi=10.1007/s00436-002-0799-9 |pmid=12743807 |s2cid=35019516}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Burri C, Brun R |date=June 2003 |title=Eflornithine for the treatment of human African trypanosomiasis |journal=Parasitology Research |volume=90 Supp 1 |pages=S49–S52 |doi=10.1007/s00436-002-0766-5 |pmid=12811548 |s2cid=35509112}}</ref> These drugs are not fully effective and are toxic to humans.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Docampo R, Moreno SN |date=June 2003 |title=Current chemotherapy of human African trypanosomiasis |journal=Parasitology Research |volume=90 Supp 1 |pages=S10–S13 |doi=10.1007/s00436-002-0752-y |pmid=12811544 |s2cid=21917230}}</ref> In addition, drug resistance has developed in the parasites against all the drugs.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Barrett MP, Vincent IM, Burchmore RJ, Kazibwe AJ, Matovu E |date=September 2011 |title=Drug resistance in human African trypanosomiasis |journal=Future Microbiology |volume=6 |issue=9 |pages=1037–1047 |doi=10.2217/fmb.11.88 |pmid=21958143}}</ref> The drugs are of limited application since they are effective against specific strains of ''T. brucei'' and the life cycle stages of the parasites. Suramin is used only for first-stage infection of ''T. b. rhodesiense'',  pentamidine for first-stage infection of ''T. b. gambiense'', and eflornithine for second-stage infection of ''T. b. gambiense''. Melarsopol is the only drug effective against the two types of parasite in both infection stages,<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Babokhov P, Sanyaolu AO, Oyibo WA, Fagbenro-Beyioku AF, Iriemenam NC |date=July 2013 |title=A current analysis of chemotherapy strategies for the treatment of human African trypanosomiasis |journal=Pathogens and Global Health |volume=107 |issue=5 |pages=242–252 |doi=10.1179/2047773213Y.0000000105 |pmc=4001453 |pmid=23916333}}</ref> but is highly toxic, such that 5% of treated individuals die of brain damage ([[Encephalopathy|reactive encephalopathy]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Kennedy PG |date=February 2013 |title=Clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment of human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness) |journal=The Lancet. Neurology |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=186–194 |doi=10.1016/S1474-4422(12)70296-X |pmid=23260189 |s2cid=8688394}}</ref> Another drug, [[nifurtimox]], recommended for [[Chagas disease]] (American trypanosomiasis), is itself a weak drug but in combination with melarsopol, it is used as the first-line medication against second-stage infection of ''T. b. gambiense.''<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Lutje V, Seixas J, Kennedy A |date=June 2013 |title=Chemotherapy for second-stage human African trypanosomiasis |journal=The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews |volume=2013 |issue=6 |article-number=CD006201 |doi=10.1002/14651858.CD006201.pub3 |pmc=6532745 |pmid=23807762}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Bottieau E, Clerinx J |date=March 2019 |title=Human African Trypanosomiasis: Progress and Stagnation |journal=Infectious Disease Clinics of North America |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=61–77 |doi=10.1016/j.idc.2018.10.003 |pmid=30712768 |s2cid=73432597}}</ref>

Historically, arsenic and mercuric compounds were introduced in the early 20th century, with success particularly in animal infections.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Thomas HW |date=May 1905 |title=Some Experiments in the Treatment of Trypanosomiasis |journal=British Medical Journal |volume=1 |issue=2317 |pages=1140–1143 |doi=10.1136/bmj.1.2317.1140 |pmc=2320665 |pmid=20762118}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Moore B, Nierenstein M, Todd JL |date=1907 |title=On the Treatment of Trypanosomiasis by Atoxyl (an Organic Arsenical Compound), followed by a Mercuric Salt (Mercuric Chloride) being a Bio-Chemical Study of the Reaction of a Parasitic Protozoon to Different Chemical Reagents at Different Stages of its Life History |journal=The Biochemical Journal |volume=2 |issue=5–6 |pages=300–324 |doi=10.1042/bj0020300 |pmc=1276215 |pmid=16742071}}</ref> German physician [[Paul Ehrlich]] and his Japanese associate [[Kiyoshi Shiga]] developed the first specific trypanocidal drug in 1904 from a dye, trypan red, which they named Trypanroth.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Wenyon CM |date=April 1907 |title=Action of the Colours of Benzidine on Mice Infected with Trypanosoma dimorphon |journal=The Journal of Hygiene |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=273–290 |doi=10.1017/s0022172400033295 |pmc=2236235 |pmid=20474312}}</ref> These chemical preparations were effective only at high and toxic dosages, and were not suitable for clinical use.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Nocht B |date=1935 |title=Present state of knowledge of chemotherapy |url=https://mednexus.org/doi/10.5555/cmj.0366-6999.49.05.p479.01 |journal=Chinese Medical Journal |language=en |volume=49 |issue=5 |pages=479–489 }}</ref>

Animal trypanosomiasis is treated with six drugs: [[diminazene aceturate]], homidium (homidium bromide and homidium chloride), [[isometamidium chloride]], [[melarsomine]], [[quinapyramine]], and suramin. They are all highly toxic to animals,<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Giordani F, Morrison LJ, Rowan TG, DE Koning HP, Barrett MP |date=December 2016 |title=The animal trypanosomiases and their chemotherapy: a review |journal=Parasitology |volume=143 |issue=14 |pages=1862–1889 |doi=10.1017/S0031182016001268 |pmc=5142301 |pmid=27719692}}</ref> and drug resistance is prevalent.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Kasozi KI, MacLeod ET, Waiswa C, Mahero M, Ntulume I, Welburn SC |date=August 2022 |title=Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Knowledge Attitude and Practices on African Animal Trypanocide Resistance |journal=Tropical Medicine and Infectious Disease |volume=7 |issue=9 |page=205 |doi=10.3390/tropicalmed7090205 |pmc=9503918 |pmid=36136616 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Homidium is the first prescription anti-trypanosomal drug. It was developed as a modified compound of phenantridine, which was found in 1938 to have trypanocidal activity against the bovine parasite, ''[[Trypanosoma congolense|T. congolense]].''<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Walls LP |date=1947 |title=The chemotherapy of phenanthridine compounds |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jctb.5000660604 |journal=Journal of the Society of Chemical Industry |language=en |volume=66 |issue=6 |pages=182–187 |doi=10.1002/jctb.5000660604 |archive-date=4 October 2022 |access-date=30 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221004043811/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jctb.5000660604 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Among its products, dimidium bromide and its derivatives were first used in 1948 in animal cases in Africa,<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Wilson SG |date=April 1948 |title=Further observations on the curative value of dimidium bromide in Trypanosoma congolense infections in bovines in Uganda |journal=The Journal of Comparative Pathology and Therapeutics |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=94–106 |doi=10.1016/s0368-1742(48)80008-1 |pmid=18861668}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Wilson SG |date=1948 |title=Further Observations on the Curative Value of Dimidium Bromide (Phenanthridinium 1553) in Trypanosoma Congolense Infections in Bovines in Uganda |journal=Journal of Comparative Pathology and Therapeutics |language=en |volume=58 |issue=2 |pages=94–106 |doi=10.1016/S0368-1742(48)80008-1 |pmid=18861668}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Carmichael J |date=April 1950 |title=Dimidium bromide or phenanthridinium 1553; a note on the present position |journal=The Veterinary Record |volume=62 |issue=17 |page=257 |doi=10.1136/vr.62.17.257-a |doi-broken-date=19 June 2026 |pmid=15418753 |s2cid=33016283}}</ref> and became known as homidium (or as [[ethidium bromide]] in molecular biology<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Lai JS, Herr W |date=August 1992 |title=Ethidium bromide provides a simple tool for identifying genuine DNA-independent protein associations |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=89 |issue=15 |pages=6958–6962 |bibcode=1992PNAS...89.6958L |doi=10.1073/pnas.89.15.6958 |pmc=49624 |pmid=1495986 |doi-access=free}}</ref>).<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Elslager EF, Thompson PE |date=1962 |title=Parasite Chemotherapy |journal=Annual Review of Pharmacology |language=en |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=193–214 |doi=10.1146/annurev.pa.02.040162.001205 |issn=0066-4251}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Kasozi KI, MacLeod ET, Ntulume I, Welburn SC |date=2022 |title=An Update on African Trypanocide Pharmaceutics and Resistance |journal=Frontiers in Veterinary Science |volume=9 |article-number=828111 |doi=10.3389/fvets.2022.828111 |pmc=8959112 |pmid=35356785 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Drug development ===

The major challenge against the human disease has been to find drugs that readily pass the blood-brain barrier. The latest drug that has come into clinical use is fexinidazol, but promising results have also been obtained with the benzoxaborole drug [[acoziborole]] (SCYX-7158). This drug is currently under evaluation as a single-dose oral treatment, which is a great advantage compared to currently used drugs. Another research field that has been extensively studied in ''Trypanosoma brucei'' is to target its nucleotide metabolism.<ref name="Hofer2023">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Hofer A |date=2022 |title=Targeting the nucleotide metabolism of Trypanosoma brucei and other trypanosomatids. |journal=FEMS Microbiology Reviews |volume=47 |issue=3 |article-number=fuad020 |doi=10.1093/femsre/fuad020 |pmc=10208901 |pmid=37156497 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The nucleotide metabolism studies have both led to the development of adenosine analogues looking promising in animal studies, and to the finding that downregulation of the P2 adenosine transporter is a common way to acquire partial drug resistance against the melaminophenyl arsenical and [[diamidine]] drug families (containing melarsoprol and pentamidine, respectively).<ref name="Hofer2023" /> This is particularly a problem with the veterinary drug diminazene aceturate. Drug uptake and degradation are two major issues to consider to avoid drug resistance development.  In the case of nucleoside analogues, they need to be taken up by the P1 nucleoside transporter (instead of P2), and they also need to be resistant against cleavage in the parasite.<ref name="pmid27036940">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Vodnala M, Ranjbarian F, Pavlova A, de Koning HP, Hofer A |date=2016 |title=Methylthioadenosine Phosphorylase Protects the Parasite from the Antitrypanosomal Effect of Deoxyadenosine: implications for the pharmacology of adenosine antimetabolites |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=291 |issue=22 |pages=11717–26 |doi=10.1074/jbc.M116.715615 |pmc=4882440 |pmid=27036940 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="pmid28373184">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Ranjbarian F, Vodnala M, Alzahrani KJ, Ebiloma GU, de Koning HP, Hofer A |date=2016 |title=9-(2'-Deoxy-2'-Fluoro-β-d-Arabinofuranosyl) Adenine Is a Potent Antitrypanosomal Adenosine Analogue That Circumvents Transport-Related Drug Resistance |journal=Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy |volume=61 |issue=6 |article-number=e02719-16 |doi=10.1128/AAC.02719-16 |pmc=5444181 |pmid=28373184 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

'''Phytochemicals.''' Some [[phytochemical]]s have shown research promise against the ''T. b. brucei'' strain.<ref name="Ibrahim-et-al-2014">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Ibrahim MA, Mohammed A, Isah MB, Aliyu AB |date=May 2014 |title=Anti-trypanosomal activity of African medicinal plants: a review update |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |publisher=[[International Society of Ethnopharmacology]] ([[Elsevier]]) |volume=154 |issue=1 |pages=26–54 |doi=10.1016/j.jep.2014.04.012 |pmid=24742753}}</ref> Aderbauer ''et al.'', 2008 and Umar ''et al.'', 2010 find ''[[Khaya senegalensis]]'' is effective [[in vitro]] and Ibrahim ''et al.'', 2013 and 2008 [[in vivo]] (in [[laboratory rat|rats]]).<ref name="Ibrahim-et-al-2014" /> Ibrahim ''et al.'', 2013 find a lower dose reduces [[parasitemia]] by this subspecies and a higher dose is curative and prevents injury.<ref name="Ibrahim-et-al-2014" />
