''T. brucei'' is found where its tsetse fly vectors are prevalent in continental Africa. That is to say, tropical rainforest ([[Köppen climate classification#Af|Af]]), tropical monsoon ([[Köppen climate classification#Am|Am]]), and tropical savannah ([[Köppen climate classification#Aw|Aw]]) areas of continental Africa.<ref name=fao/> Hence, the equatorial region of Africa is called the "sleeping sickness" belt. However, the specific type of the trypanosome differs according to geography. ''T. b. rhodesiense'' is found primarily in East Africa, while ''T. b. gambiense'' is found in Central and West Africa.

==Impact==
''T. brucei'' is a major cause of [[livestock disease]] in [[sub-Saharan Africa]].<ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" /><ref name="Auty-et-al-2015">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Auty H, Torr SJ, Michoel T, Jayaraman S, Morrison LJ |date=August 2015 |title=Cattle trypanosomosis: the diversity of trypanosomes and implications for disease epidemiology and control |journal=Revue Scientifique et Technique |publisher=O.I.E ([[World Organisation for Animal Health]]) |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=587–598 |doi=10.20506/rst.34.2.2382 |pmid=26601459 |s2cid=42700199 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It is thus of tremendous [[veterinary parasitology|veterinary concern]] and one of the greatest limitations on [[agriculture in Africa]] and the economic life of sub-Saharan Africa.<ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" /><ref name="Auty-et-al-2015" />

==Evolution==
''Trypanosoma brucei gambiense'' evolved from a single progenitor ~10,000 years ago.<ref name="Weir2016">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Weir W, Capewell P, Foth B, Clucas C, Pountain A, Steketee P, Veitch N, Koffi M, De Meeûs T, Kaboré J, Camara M, Cooper A, Tait A, Jamonneau V, Bucheton B, Berriman M, MacLeod A |date=January 2016 |title=Population genomics reveals the origin and asexual evolution of human infective trypanosomes |journal=eLife |volume=5 |article-number=e11473 |doi=10.7554/eLife.11473 |pmc=4739771 |pmid=26809473 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It is evolving asexually and its genome shows the [[Meselson effect]].<ref name="Weir2016" />

==Genetics==
There are two subpopulations of  ''T. b. gambiense'' that possesses two distinct groups that differ in genotype and phenotype. Group 2 is more akin to ''T. b. brucei'' than group 1 ''T. b. gambiense''.<ref name="Paindavoine1986">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Paindavoine P, Pays E, Laurent M, Geltmeyer Y, Le Ray D, Mehlitz D, Steinert M |date=February 1986 |title=The use of DNA hybridization and numerical taxonomy in determining relationships between Trypanosoma brucei stocks and subspecies |journal=Parasitology |volume=92 |issue=Pt 1 |pages=31–50 |doi=10.1017/S0031182000063435 |pmid=3960593 |s2cid=33529173}}</ref>

All ''T. b. gambiense''  are resistant to killing by a serum component — trypanosome lytic factor (TLF) of which there are two types: TLF-1 and TLF-2. Group 1 ''T. b. gambiense'' parasites avoid uptake of the TLF particles while those of group 2 are able to either neutralize or compensate for the effects of TLF.<ref name="Capewell2011">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Capewell P, Veitch NJ, Turner CM, Raper J, Berriman M, Hajduk SL, MacLeod A |date=September 2011 |title=Differences between Trypanosoma brucei gambiense groups 1 and 2 in their resistance to killing by trypanolytic factor 1 |journal=PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases |volume=5 |issue=9 |article-number=e1287 |doi=10.1371/journal.pntd.0001287 |pmc=3167774 |pmid=21909441 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In contrast, resistance in ''T. b. rhodesiense'' is dependent upon the expression of a serum resistance associated (SRA) gene.<ref name="Lecordier2009">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Lecordier L, Vanhollebeke B, Poelvoorde P, Tebabi P, Paturiaux-Hanocq F, Andris F, Lins L, Pays E |date=December 2009 |title=C-terminal mutants of apolipoprotein L-I efficiently kill both Trypanosoma brucei brucei and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense |journal=PLOS Pathogens |volume=5 |issue=12 |article-number=e1000685 |doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.1000685 |pmc=2778949 |pmid=19997494 |doi-access=free |veditors=Mansfield JM}}</ref> This gene is not found in ''T. b. gambiense''.<ref name="DeGreef1989">{{Cite journal |vauthors=De Greef C, Imberechts H, Matthyssens G, Van Meirvenne N, Hamers R |date=September 1989 |title=A gene expressed only in serum-resistant variants of Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense |journal=Molecular and Biochemical Parasitology |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=169–176 |doi=10.1016/0166-6851(89)90189-8 |pmid=2528066}}</ref>

===Genome===
The [[genome]] of ''T. brucei'' is made up of:<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Ogbadoyi E, Ersfeld K, Robinson D, Sherwin T, Gull K |date=March 2000 |title=Architecture of the Trypanosoma brucei nucleus during interphase and mitosis |journal=Chromosoma |volume=108 |issue=8 |pages=501–513 |doi=10.1007/s004120050402 |pmid=10794572 |s2cid=3850480}}</ref>
* 11 pairs of large [[chromosome]]s of 1 to 6 megabase pairs.
* 3–5 intermediate chromosomes of 200 to 500 kilobase pairs.
* Around 100 minichromosomes of around 50 to 100 kilobase pairs. These may be present in multiple copies per [[haploid]] genome.
Most [[genes]] are held on the large chromosomes, with the minichromosomes carrying only ''VSG'' genes. The genome has been sequenced and is available on [[GeneDB]].<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Jackson AP, Sanders M, Berry A, McQuillan J, Aslett MA, Quail MA, Chukualim B, Capewell P, MacLeod A, Melville SE, Gibson W, Barry JD, Berriman M, Hertz-Fowler C |date=April 2010 |title=The genome sequence of Trypanosoma brucei gambiense, causative agent of chronic human african trypanosomiasis |journal=PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases |volume=4 |issue=4 |article-number=e658 |doi=10.1371/journal.pntd.0000658 |pmc=2854126 |pmid=20404998 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The mitochondrial genome is found condensed into the [[kinetoplast]], an unusual feature unique to the kinetoplastid protozoans. The kinetoplast and the [[basal body]] of the [[flagellum]] are strongly associated via a cytoskeletal structure<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Ogbadoyi EO, Robinson DR, Gull K |date=May 2003 |title=A high-order trans-membrane structural linkage is responsible for mitochondrial genome positioning and segregation by flagellar basal bodies in trypanosomes |journal=Molecular Biology of the Cell |volume=14 |issue=5 |pages=1769–1779 |doi=10.1091/mbc.E02-08-0525 |pmc=165075 |pmid=12802053}}</ref>

In 1993, a new base, ß-d-glucopyranosyloxymethyluracil ([[base J]]), was identified in the nuclear DNA of ''T. brucei.''<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Borst P, Sabatini R |date=2008 |title=Base J: discovery, biosynthesis, and possible functions |journal=Annual Review of Microbiology |volume=62 |pages=235–251 |doi=10.1146/annurev.micro.62.081307.162750 |pmid=18729733}}</ref>

== VSG coat ==
{{Main| Variant surface glycoprotein}}
The surface of ''T. brucei'' and other species of trypanosomes is covered by a dense external coat called variant surface glycoprotein (VSG).<ref name="Barry">{{Cite book |title=Advances in Parasitology Volume 49 |vauthors=Barry JD, McCulloch R |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-12-031749-3 |volume=<!-- --> |pages=1–70 |chapter=Antigenic variation in trypanosomes: enhanced phenotypic variation in a eukaryotic parasite |doi=10.1016/S0065-308X(01)49037-3 |pmid=11461029}}</ref> VSGs are 60-kDa proteins which are densely packed (~5 million molecules) to form a 12–15 nm surface coat. VSG dimers make up about 90% of all cell surface proteins in trypanosomes. They also make up ~10% of total cell protein. For this reason, these proteins are highly immunogenic and an immune response raised against a specific VSG coat will rapidly kill trypanosomes expressing this variant. However, with each cell division there is a possibility that the progeny will switch expression to change the VSG that is being expressed.<ref name="Barry"/><ref name="Morrison-et-al-2009">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Morrison LJ, Marcello L, McCulloch R |date=December 2009 |title=Antigenic variation in the African trypanosome: molecular mechanisms and phenotypic complexity |journal=Cellular Microbiology |volume=11 |issue=12 |pages=1724–1734 |doi=10.1111/j.1462-5822.2009.01383.x |pmid=19751359 |s2cid=26552797 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

This VSG coat enables an infecting ''T. brucei'' population to persistently evade the host's [[immune system]], allowing chronic infection. VSG is highly [[immunogenic]], and an [[adaptive immunity|immune response]] raised against a specific VSG coat rapidly kills trypanosomes expressing this variant. [[Antibody]]-mediated trypanosome killing can also be observed [[in vitro]] by a [[complement system|complement-mediated]] [[lysis]] [[assay]]. However, with each [[cell division]] there is a possibility that one or both of the [[offspring|progeny]] will switch expression to change the VSG that is being expressed. The frequency of VSG switching has been measured to be approximately 0.1% per division.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Turner CM |date=August 1997 |title=The rate of antigenic variation in fly-transmitted and syringe-passaged infections of Trypanosoma brucei |journal=FEMS Microbiology Letters |volume=153 |issue=1 |pages=227–231 |doi=10.1111/j.1574-6968.1997.tb10486.x |pmid=9252591}}</ref>  As ''T. brucei'' populations can peak at a size of 10<sup>11</sup> within a host<ref name="Barry2012">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Barry JD, Hall JP, Plenderleith L |date=September 2012 |title=Genome hyperevolution and the success of a parasite |journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences |volume=1267 |issue=1 |pages=11–17 |bibcode=2012NYASA1267...11B |doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.2012.06654.x |pmc=3467770 |pmid=22954210}}</ref> this rapid rate of switching ensures that the parasite population is typically highly diverse.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Hall JP, Wang H, Barry JD |date=11 July 2013 |title=Mosaic VSGs and the scale of Trypanosoma brucei antigenic variation |journal=PLOS Pathogens |volume=9 |issue=7 |article-number=e1003502 |doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.1003502 |pmc=3708902 |pmid=23853603 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Mugnier MR, Cross GA, Papavasiliou FN |date=March 2015 |title=The in vivo dynamics of antigenic variation in Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Science |volume=347 |issue=6229 |pages=1470–1473 |bibcode=2015Sci...347.1470M |doi=10.1126/science.aaa4502 |pmc=4514441 |pmid=25814582}}</ref> Because host immunity against a specific VSG does not develop immediately, some parasites will have switched to an antigenically distinct VSG variant, and can go on to multiply and continue the infection. The clinical effect of this cycle is successive 'waves' of [[parasitemia]] (trypanosomes in the blood).<ref name="Barry" />

Expression of ''VSG'' genes occurs through a number of mechanisms yet to be fully understood.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Pays E |date=November 2005 |title=Regulation of antigen gene expression in Trypanosoma brucei |journal=Trends in Parasitology |volume=21 |issue=11 |pages=517–520 |doi=10.1016/j.pt.2005.08.016 |pmid=16126458}}</ref> The expressed VSG can be switched either by activating a different expression site (and thus changing to express the ''VSG'' in that site), or by changing the ''VSG'' gene in the active site to a different variant. The genome contains many hundreds if not thousands of ''VSG'' genes, both on minichromosomes and in repeated sections ('arrays') in the interior of the chromosomes. These are transcriptionally silent, typically with omitted sections or premature stop codons, but are important in the evolution of new VSG genes. It is estimated up to 10% of the ''T. brucei'' genome may be made up of VSG genes or [[pseudogenes]]. It is thought that any of these genes can be moved into the active site by [[Genetic recombination|recombination]] for expression.<ref name="Morrison-et-al-2009" /> VSG silencing is largely due to the effects of [[histone]] variants H3.V and H4.V. These histones cause changes in the three-dimensional structure of the ''T. brucei'' genome that results in a lack of expression. VSG genes are typically located in the subtelomeric regions of the chromosomes, which makes it easier for them to be silenced when they are not being used.<ref name="F1000-of-Mueller">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Rudenko G |date=2018-10-26 |title=Faculty of 1000 evaluation for Genome organization and DNA accessibility control antigenic variation in trypanosomes |doi=10.3410/f.734240334.793552268 |doi-access=free |website=[[Faculty of 1000|F1000]]}}</ref><ref name="Mueller-et-al-2018">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Müller LS, Cosentino RO, Förstner KU, Guizetti J, Wedel C, Kaplan N, Janzen CJ, Arampatzi P, Vogel J, Steinbiss S, Otto TD, Saliba AE, Sebra RP, Siegel TN |date=November 2018 |title=Genome organization and DNA accessibility control antigenic variation in trypanosomes |journal=Nature |publisher=[[Nature Research]] |volume=563 |issue=7729 |pages=121–125 |bibcode=2018Natur.563..121M |doi=10.1038/s41586-018-0619-8 |pmc=6784898 |pmid=30333624 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It remains unproven whether the regulation of VSG switching is purely stochastic or whether environmental stimuli affect switching frequency. Switching is linked to two factors: variation in activation of individual VSG genes; and differentiation to the "short stumpy" stage - triggered by conditions of high population density - which is the nonreproductive, interhost transmission stage.<ref name="Mideo-et-al-2013" /> {{As of|2021}} it also remains unexplained how this transition is timed and how the next surface protein gene is chosen.<ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" /> These questions of antigenic variation in ''T. brucei'' and other parasites are among the most interesting in the field of [[infection]].<ref name="Luzak-et-al-2021" />

==Killing by human serum and resistance to human serum killing==
''Trypanosoma brucei brucei'' is not human infective because it is susceptible to [[innate|innate immune system]] 'trypanolytic' factors present in the serum of some primates, including humans. These trypanolytic factors have been identified as two serum complexes designated trypanolytic factors (TLF-1 and −2) both of which contain [[haptoglobin-related protein]] (HPR) and [[APOL1|apolipoprotein LI]] (ApoL1). TLF-1 is a member of the [[high density lipoprotein]] family of particles while TLF-2 is a related high molecular weight serum protein binding complex.<ref name="Hajduk1989">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Hajduk SL, Moore DR, Vasudevacharya J, Siqueira H, Torri AF, Tytler EM, Esko JD |date=March 1989 |title=Lysis of Trypanosoma brucei by a toxic subspecies of human high density lipoprotein |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=264 |issue=9 |pages=5210–5217 |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)83720-6 |pmid=2494183 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Raper1999">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Raper J, Fung R, Ghiso J, Nussenzweig V, Tomlinson S |date=April 1999 |title=Characterization of a novel trypanosome lytic factor from human serum |journal=Infection and Immunity |volume=67 |issue=4 |pages=1910–1916 |doi=10.1128/IAI.67.4.1910-1916.1999 |pmc=96545 |pmid=10085035}}</ref> The protein components of TLF-1 are haptoglobin related protein (HPR), apolipoprotein L-1 (apoL-1) and apolipoprotein A-1 (apoA-1). These three proteins are colocalized within spherical particles containing phospholipids and cholesterol. The protein components of TLF-2 include IgM and apolipoprotein A-I.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Vanhollebeke B, Pays E |date=May 2010 |title=The trypanolytic factor of human serum: many ways to enter the parasite, a single way to kill |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00552632/file/PEER_stage2_10.1111%252Fj.1365-2958.2010.07156.x.pdf |journal=Molecular Microbiology |volume=76 |issue=4 |pages=806–814 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2958.2010.07156.x |pmid=20398209 |s2cid=7740199 |archive-date=30 September 2022 |access-date=30 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220930125645/https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00552632/file/PEER_stage2_10.1111%252Fj.1365-2958.2010.07156.x.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

Trypanolytic factors are found only in a few species, including humans, [[gorilla]]s, [[mandrill]]s, [[baboon]]s and [[sooty mangabey]]s. This appears to be because haptoglobin-related protein and apolipoprotein L-1 are unique to primates. This suggests these genes originated in the primate genome {{Ma|25}}-{{Ma|35}}.<ref name="Lugli2004">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Lugli EB, Pouliot M, ((Portela Md)), Loomis MR, Raper J |date=November 2004 |title=Characterization of primate trypanosome lytic factors |journal=Molecular and Biochemical Parasitology |volume=138 |issue=1 |pages=9–20 |doi=10.1016/j.molbiopara.2004.07.004 |pmid=15500911}}</ref>

Human infective subspecies ''T. b. gambiense'' and ''T. b. rhodesiense'' have evolved mechanisms of resisting the trypanolytic factors, described below.

===ApoL1===
[[APOL1|ApoL1]] is a member of a six gene family, ApoL1-6, that have arisen by tandem duplication. These proteins are normally involved in host apoptosis or autophagic death and possess a Bcl-2 homology domain 3.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Vanhollebeke B, Pays E |date=September 2006 |title=The function of apolipoproteins L |journal=Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences |volume=63 |issue=17 |pages=1937–1944 |doi=10.1007/s00018-006-6091-x |pmc=11136045 |pmid=16847577 |s2cid=12713960}}</ref> [[APOL1|ApoL1]] has been identified as the toxic component involved in trypanolysis.<ref name="Vanhamme2003">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Vanhamme L, Paturiaux-Hanocq F, Poelvoorde P, Nolan DP, Lins L, Van Den Abbeele J, Pays A, Tebabi P, Van Xong H, Jacquet A, Moguilevsky N, Dieu M, Kane JP, De Baetselier P, Brasseur R, Pays E |date=March 2003 |title=Apolipoprotein L-I is the trypanosome lytic factor of human serum |journal=Nature |volume=422 |issue=6927 |pages=83–87 |bibcode=2003Natur.422...83V |doi=10.1038/nature01461 |pmid=12621437 |s2cid=4310920}}</ref> ApoLs have been subject to recent selective evolution possibly related to resistance to pathogens.<ref name="Smith2009">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Smith EE, Malik HS |date=May 2009 |title=The apolipoprotein L family of programmed cell death and immunity genes rapidly evolved in primates at discrete sites of host-pathogen interactions |journal=Genome Research |volume=19 |issue=5 |pages=850–858 |doi=10.1101/gr.085647.108 |pmc=2675973 |pmid=19299565}}</ref>

The gene encoding [[APOL1|ApoL1]] is found on the long arm of [[chromosome 22]] (22q12.3). Variants of this gene, termed G1 and G2, provide protection against ''T. b. rhodesiense''.<ref name=Genovese2010/> These benefits are not without their downside as a specific [[APOL1|ApoL1]] [[glomerulopathy]] has been identified.<ref name="Genovese2010">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Genovese G, Friedman DJ, Ross MD, Lecordier L, Uzureau P, Freedman BI, Bowden DW, Langefeld CD, Oleksyk TK, Uscinski Knob AL, Bernhardy AJ, Hicks PJ, Nelson GW, Vanhollebeke B, Winkler CA, Kopp JB, Pays E, Pollak MR |date=August 2010 |title=Association of trypanolytic ApoL1 variants with kidney disease in African Americans |journal=Science |volume=329 |issue=5993 |pages=841–845 |bibcode=2010Sci...329..841G |doi=10.1126/science.1193032 |pmc=2980843 |pmid=20647424}}</ref><ref name="Wasser2012">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Wasser WG, Tzur S, Wolday D, Adu D, Baumstein D, Rosset S, Skorecki K |year=2012 |title=Population genetics of chronic kidney disease: the evolving story of APOL1 |journal=Journal of Nephrology |volume=25 |issue=5 |pages=603–618 |doi=10.5301/jn.5000179 |doi-broken-date=19 June 2026 |pmid=22878977}}</ref> This glomerulopathy may help to explain the greater prevalence of [[hypertension]] in African populations.<ref>{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Lipkowitz MS, Freedman BI, Langefeld CD, Comeau ME, Bowden DW, Kao WH, Astor BC, Bottinger EP, Iyengar SK, Klotman PE, Freedman RG, Zhang W, Parekh RS, Choi MJ, Nelson GW, Winkler CA, Kopp JB |date=January 2013 |title=Apolipoprotein L1 gene variants associate with hypertension-attributed nephropathy and the rate of kidney function decline in African Americans |journal=Kidney International |volume=83 |issue=1 |pages=114–120 |doi=10.1038/ki.2012.263 |pmc=3484228 |pmid=22832513}}</ref>

The gene encodes a protein of 383 residues, including a typical signal peptide of 12 amino acids.<ref name="Duchateau1997">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Duchateau PN, Pullinger CR, Orellana RE, Kunitake ST, Naya-Vigne J, O'Connor PM, Malloy MJ, Kane JP |date=October 1997 |title=Apolipoprotein L, a new human high density lipoprotein apolipoprotein expressed by the pancreas. Identification, cloning, characterization, and plasma distribution of apolipoprotein L |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=272 |issue=41 |pages=25576–25582 |doi=10.1074/jbc.272.41.25576 |pmid=9325276 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The plasma protein is a single chain polypeptide with an apparent molecular mass of 42 kilodaltons. [[APOL1|ApoL1]] has a membrane pore forming domain functionally similar to that of bacterial [[colicin]]s.<ref name="Pérez-Morga2005">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Pérez-Morga D, Vanhollebeke B, Paturiaux-Hanocq F, Nolan DP, Lins L, Homblé F, Vanhamme L, Tebabi P, Pays A, Poelvoorde P, Jacquet A, Brasseur R, Pays E |date=July 2005 |title=Apolipoprotein L-I promotes trypanosome lysis by forming pores in lysosomal membranes |journal=Science |volume=309 |issue=5733 |pages=469–472 |bibcode=2005Sci...309..469P |doi=10.1126/science.1114566 |pmid=16020735 |s2cid=33189804}}</ref> This domain is flanked by the membrane addressing domain and both these domains are required for parasite killing.

Within the kidney, [[APOL1|ApoL1]] is found in the [[podocyte]]s in the [[glomerulus (kidney)|glomeruli]], the proximal tubular epithelium and the arteriolar endothelium.<ref name="Madhavan2011">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Madhavan SM, O'Toole JF, Konieczkowski M, Ganesan S, Bruggeman LA, Sedor JR |date=November 2011 |title=APOL1 localization in normal kidney and nondiabetic kidney disease |journal=Journal of the American Society of Nephrology |volume=22 |issue=11 |pages=2119–2128 |doi=10.1681/ASN.2011010069 |pmc=3231786 |pmid=21997392}}</ref> It has a high affinity for [[phosphatidic acid]] and [[cardiolipin]] and can be induced by [[interferon]] gamma and [[tumor necrosis factor]] alpha.<ref name="Zhaorigetu2008">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Zhaorigetu S, Wan G, Kaini R, Jiang Z, Hu CA |date=November 2008 |title=ApoL1, a BH3-only lipid-binding protein, induces autophagic cell death |journal=Autophagy |volume=4 |issue=8 |pages=1079–1082 |doi=10.4161/auto.7066 |pmc=2659410 |pmid=18927493}}</ref>

===Hpr===
Hpr is 91% identical to [[haptoglobin]] (Hp), an abundant acute phase serum protein, which possesses a high affinity for [[hemoglobin]] (Hb). When Hb is released from erythrocytes undergoing intravascular hemolysis Hp forms a complex with the Hb and these are removed from circulation by the [[CD163]] scavenger receptor. In contrast to Hp–Hb, the Hpr–Hb complex does not bind CD163 and the Hpr serum concentration appears to be unaffected by hemolysis.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Widener J, Nielsen MJ, Shiflett A, Moestrup SK, Hajduk S |date=September 2007 |title=Hemoglobin is a co-factor of human trypanosome lytic factor |journal=PLOS Pathogens |volume=3 |issue=9 |pages=1250–1261 |doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.0030129 |pmc=1971115 |pmid=17845074 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Killing mechanism===
The association of HPR with hemoglobin allows TLF-1 binding and uptake via the trypanosome haptoglobin-hemoglobin receptor (TbHpHbR).<ref name="Vanhollebeke2008">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Vanhollebeke B, De Muylder G, Nielsen MJ, Pays A, Tebabi P, Dieu M, Raes M, Moestrup SK, Pays E |date=May 2008 |title=A haptoglobin-hemoglobin receptor conveys innate immunity to Trypanosoma brucei in humans |journal=Science |volume=320 |issue=5876 |pages=677–681 |bibcode=2008Sci...320..677V |doi=10.1126/science.1156296 |pmid=18451305 |s2cid=206512161}}</ref> TLF-2 enters trypanosomes independently of TbHpHbR.<ref name=Vanhollebeke2008/> TLF-1 uptake increases when haptoglobin level is low. TLF-1 overtakes haptoglobin and binds free hemoglobin in the serum. However the complete absence of haptoglobin is associated with a decreased killing rate by serum.<ref name="Vanhollebeke2007">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Vanhollebeke B, Nielsen MJ, Watanabe Y, Truc P, Vanhamme L, Nakajima K, Moestrup SK, Pays E |date=March 2007 |title=Distinct roles of haptoglobin-related protein and apolipoprotein L-I in trypanolysis by human serum |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=104 |issue=10 |pages=4118–4123 |bibcode=2007PNAS..104.4118V |doi=10.1073/pnas.0609902104 |pmc=1820718 |pmid=17360487 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

The trypanosome haptoglobin-hemoglobin receptor is an elongated three a-helical bundle with a small membrane distal head.<ref name="Higgins2013">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Higgins MK, Tkachenko O, Brown A, Reed J, Raper J, Carrington M |date=January 2013 |title=Structure of the trypanosome haptoglobin-hemoglobin receptor and implications for nutrient uptake and innate immunity |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=110 |issue=5 |pages=1905–1910 |bibcode=2013PNAS..110.1905H |doi=10.1073/pnas.1214943110 |pmc=3562850 |pmid=23319650 |doi-access=free}}</ref> This protein extends above the variant surface glycoprotein layer that surrounds the parasite.

The first step in the killing mechanism is the binding of TLF to high affinity receptors—the haptoglobin-hemoglobin receptors—that are located in the flagellar pocket of the parasite.<ref name=Vanhollebeke2008/><ref name="Green2003">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Green HP, Del Pilar Molina Portela M, St Jean EN, Lugli EB, Raper J |date=January 2003 |title=Evidence for a Trypanosoma brucei lipoprotein scavenger receptor |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=278 |issue=1 |pages=422–427 |doi=10.1074/jbc.M207215200 |pmid=12401813 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The bound TLF is endocytosed via coated vesicles and then trafficked to the parasite [[lysosome]]s. [[APOL1|ApoL1]] is the main lethal factor in the TLFs and kills trypanosomes after insertion into [[endosome|endosomal]] / [[lysosome|lysosomal]] membranes.<ref name=Vanhamme2003/> After ingestion by the parasite, the TLF-1 particle is trafficked to the [[lysosome]] wherein ApoL1 is activated by a pH mediated conformational change. After fusion with the [[lysosome]] the pH drops from ~7 to ~5. This induces a conformational change in the [[APOL1|ApoL1]] membrane addressing domain which in turn causes a salt bridge linked hinge to open. This releases [[APOL1|ApoL1]] from the HDL particle to insert in the lysosomal membrane. The [[APOL1|ApoL1]] protein then creates anionic pores in the membrane which leads to depolarization of the membrane, a continuous influx of [[chloride]] and subsequent osmotic swelling of the [[lysosome]]. This influx in its turn leads to rupture of the [[lysosome]] and the subsequent death of the parasite.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Pays E, Vanhollebeke B, Vanhamme L, Paturiaux-Hanocq F, Nolan DP, Pérez-Morga D |date=June 2006 |title=The trypanolytic factor of human serum |journal=Nature Reviews. Microbiology |volume=4 |issue=6 |pages=477–486 |doi=10.1038/nrmicro1428 |pmid=16710327 |s2cid=6151924}}</ref>

===Resistance mechanisms: ''T. b. gambiense''===
''Trypanosoma brucei gambiense'' causes 97% of human cases of sleeping sickness. Resistance to [[APOL1|ApoL1]] is principally mediated by the hydrophobic [[Beta sheet|β-sheet]] of the ''T. b. gambiense'' specific [[glycoprotein]].<ref name=Uzureau2013/> Other factors involved in resistance appear to be a change in the [[cysteine protease]] activity and TbHpHbR inactivation due to a [[leucine]] to [[serine]] substitution (L210S) at codon 210.<ref name="Uzureau2013">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Uzureau P, Uzureau S, Lecordier L, Fontaine F, Tebabi P, Homblé F, Grélard A, Zhendre V, Nolan DP, Lins L, Crowet JM, Pays A, Felu C, Poelvoorde P, Vanhollebeke B, Moestrup SK, Lyngsø J, Pedersen JS, Mottram JC, Dufourc EJ, Pérez-Morga D, Pays E |date=September 2013 |title=Mechanism of Trypanosoma brucei gambiense resistance to human serum |journal=Nature |volume=501 |issue=7467 |pages=430–434 |bibcode=2013Natur.501..430U |doi=10.1038/nature12516 |pmid=23965626 |s2cid=4400057}}</ref> This is due to a [[thymidine]] to [[cytosine]] mutation at the second codon position.<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=DeJesus E, Kieft R, Albright B, Stephens NA, Hajduk SL |year=2013 |title=A single amino acid substitution in the group 1 Trypanosoma brucei gambiense haptoglobin-hemoglobin receptor abolishes TLF-1 binding |journal=PLOS Pathogens |volume=9 |issue=4 |article-number=e1003317 |doi=10.1371/journal.ppat.1003317 |pmc=3630162 |pmid=23637606 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

These mutations may have evolved due to the coexistence of [[malaria]] where this parasite is found.<ref name=Uzureau2013/> Haptoglobin levels are low in malaria because of the hemolysis that occurs with the release of the [[merozoite]]s into the blood. The rupture of the erythrocytes results in the release of free [[heme|haem]] into the blood where it is bound by haptoglobin. The haem is then removed along with the bound haptoglobin from the blood by the [[reticuloendothelial system]].<ref>{{Cite journal |vauthors=Smith A, McCulloh RJ |date=2015 |title=Hemopexin and haptoglobin: allies against heme toxicity from hemoglobin not contenders |journal=Frontiers in Physiology |volume=6 |page=187 |doi=10.3389/fphys.2015.00187 |pmc=4485156 |pmid=26175690 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Resistance mechanisms: ''T. b. rhodesiense''===
''Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense'' relies on a different mechanism of resistance: the serum resistance associated protein (SRA). The ''SRA'' gene is a truncated version of the major and variable surface antigen of the parasite, the variant surface glycoprotein.<ref name="Pays2008">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Pays E, Vanhollebeke B |date=July 2008 |title=Mutual self-defence: the trypanolytic factor story |journal=Microbes and Infection |volume=10 |issue=9 |pages=985–989 |doi=10.1016/j.micinf.2008.07.020 |pmid=18675374 |doi-access=free}}</ref> However, it has little similarity (low sequence homology) with the VSG gene (<25%). SRA is an expression site associated gene in ''T. b. rhodesiense'' and is located upstream of the VSGs in the active telomeric expression site.<ref name="Xong1998">{{Cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Xong HV, Vanhamme L, Chamekh M, Chimfwembe CE, Van Den Abbeele J, Pays A, Van Meirvenne N, Hamers R, De Baetselier P, Pays E |date=December 1998 |title=A VSG expression site-associated gene confers resistance to human serum in Trypanosoma rhodesiense |journal=Cell |volume=95 |issue=6 |pages=839–846 |doi=10.1016/S0092-8674(00)81706-7 |pmid=9865701 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The protein is largely localized to small cytoplasmic vesicles between the flagellar pocket and the nucleus. In ''T. b. rhodesiense'' the TLF is directed to SRA containing [[endosome]]s while some dispute remains as to its presence in the [[lysosome]].<ref name=Vanhamme2003/><ref name="Shiflett2007">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Shiflett AM, Faulkner SD, Cotlin LF, Widener J, Stephens N, Hajduk SL |year=2007 |title=African trypanosomes: intracellular trafficking of host defense molecules |journal=The Journal of Eukaryotic Microbiology |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=18–21 |doi=10.1111/j.1550-7408.2006.00228.x |pmid=17300512 |s2cid=20054667}}</ref> SRA binds to [[APOL1|ApoL1]] using a coiled–coiled interaction at the ApoL1 SRA interacting domain while within the trypanosome lysosome.<ref name=Vanhamme2003/> This interaction prevents the release of the ApoL1 protein and the subsequent lysis of the lysosome and death of the parasite.

Baboons are known to be resistant to ''T. b. rhodesiense''. The baboon version of the ApoL1 gene differs from the human gene in a number of respects including two critical lysines near the C terminus that are necessary and sufficient to prevent baboon ApoL1 binding to SRA.<ref name="Thomson2009">{{Cite journal |vauthors=Thomson R, Molina-Portela P, Mott H, Carrington M, Raper J |date=November 2009 |title=Hydrodynamic gene delivery of baboon trypanosome lytic factor eliminates both animal and human-infective African trypanosomes |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=106 |issue=46 |pages=19509–19514 |bibcode=2009PNAS..10619509T |doi=10.1073/pnas.0905669106 |pmc=2780755 |pmid=19858474 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Experimental mutations allowing ApoL1 to be protected from neutralization by SRA have been shown capable of conferring trypanolytic activity on ''T. b. rhodesiense''.<ref name=Lecordier2009/> These mutations resemble those found in baboons, but also resemble natural mutations conferring protection of humans against ''T. b. rhodesiense'' which are linked to kidney disease.<ref name=Genovese2010/>

Trypanosoma brucei is a species of parasitic kinetoplastid belonging to the genus Trypanosoma that is present in sub-Saharan Africa. Unlike other protozoan parasites that normally infect blood and tissue cells, it is exclusively extracellular and inhabits the blood plasma and body fluids. It causes deadly vector-borne diseases: African trypanosomiasis or sleeping sickness in humans, and animal trypanosomiasis or nagana in cattle and horses. It is a species complex grouped into five subspecies: T. b. brucei, T. b. equiperdum, T. b. evansi, T. b. gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense. The first is a parasite of non-human mammals and causes nagana, while the latter two are zoonotic infecting both humans and animals and cause African trypanosomiasis.
T. brucei is transmitted between mammal hosts by an insect vector belonging to different species of tsetse fly (Glossina). Transmission occurs by biting during the insect's blood meal. The parasites undergo complex morphological changes as they move between insect and mammal over the course of their life cycle. The mammalian bloodstream forms are notable for their cell surface proteins, variant surface glycoproteins, which undergo remarkable antigenic variation, enabling persistent evasion of host adaptive immunity leading to chronic infection. T. brucei is one of only a few pathogens known to cross the blood-brain barrier. There is an urgent need for the development of new drug therapies, as current treatments can have severe side effects and can prove fatal to the patient.
Whilst not historically regarded as T. brucei subspecies due to their different means of transmission, clinical presentation, and loss of kinetoplast DNA, genetic analyses reveal that T. b. equiperdum and T. b. evansi are evolved from parasites very similar to T. b. brucei, and are thought to be members of the brucei clade.
The parasite was discovered in 1894 by Sir David Bruce, after whom the scientific name was given in 1899.
